title: Root ExecStartPost chmod/chown/write through swappable mktemp file in lnd-writable /run/lnd
attack_scenario: Attacker has RCE as the lnd service user (lnd is a network-facing daemon holding funds) on a node with services.btcpayserver.lightningBackend = "lnd" (the only configured macaroon user, exercised in test/tests.py). The ExecStartPost runs via nbLib.rootScript, i.e. systemd's '+' prefix: per systemd.service(5) it executes with full privileges, with User= and the file-system namespacing options (ProtectSystem, PrivateUsers, etc.) NOT applied - so it is real, unsandboxed root. $RUNTIME_DIRECTORY (/run/lnd) is owned by the lnd user (mode 711), so the attacker can unlink and replace entries in it. The attacker watches /run/lnd with inotify; when the root script's mktemp creates .btcpayserver.XXXXXX, the attacker unlinks it and plants a symlink of the same name pointing at an arbitrary target (e.g. /etc/nix-bitcoin-secrets/bitcoin-rpcpassword-privileged). The race window is attacker-controlled and seconds-long, because the intervening curl POST goes to the attacker's own lnd REST endpoint, whose response the attacker simply delays. The root script's chmod ug=r,o= and chown btcpayserver: follow the symlink, making the target file mode 440 owned by the btcpayserver user, and mv then installs the symlink as /run/lnd/btcpayserver.macaroon. btcpayserver starts after lnd, reads its 'macaroon' file, and sends the target file's contents as the Grpc-Metadata-macaroon header to the lnd REST endpoint the attacker controls - exfiltrating arbitrary root-readable files with no second compromise. The privileged RPC password grants unrestricted bitcoind RPC (empty whitelist = all methods, wallet enabled by default), i.e. on-chain fund theft. A tighter variant (win the sub-ms race between mktemp exit and the pipeline's redirect open, retryable indefinitely because Restart=on-failure re-runs ExecStartPost on each attacker-induced crash) turns the xxd-decoded, fully attacker-controlled macaroon bytes into a root arbitrary file write (e.g. rewriting /etc/passwd on default NixOS with mutableUsers), i.e. remote-to-root.
impact: secrets (privileged bitcoind RPC password, cookie, /etc/shadow, SSH keys) -> funds via unrestricted wallet RPC; racy variant gives root file write -> RCE; also root chmod/chown DoS
false_positive_risk: Would be wrong if (a) systemd on the pinned release applied fs namespacing to '+'-prefixed commands (the man page explicitly says it does not, and the script could not chown to btcpayserver at all if PrivateUsers stayed active - CI proves the chown works); (b) btcpayserver never re-reads the macaroon file (mitigated: it starts strictly after lnd, and the chmod/chown to the internet-facing btcpayserver account is already a secret-exposure primitive without the exfil channel); (c) the redirect race timing assumptions were off for the write variant - the chmod/chown/exfil variant does not depend on it. Not verified against a live VM.
recommendation: Stage the temp file outside the lnd-writable directory: replace mktemp "$RUNTIME_DIRECTORY/.${macaroon}.XXXXXX" with mktemp "/run/.${macaroon}.XXXXXX" (/run is root-owned 0755, lnd cannot create entries there), keep the chmod/chown/mv as-is (the final rename into $RUNTIME_DIRECTORY is already safe against destination symlinks). Additionally consider 'chown -h' and a post-mv verification that macaroonPath is a regular file owned by the intended user.

title: Typo 'syskernel.core_pattern' silently disables the stated core-dump kill switch
attack_scenario: The key 'syskernel.core_pattern' does not exist; systemd-sysctl logs an error for the unknown key and continues, so kernel.core_pattern keeps its NixOS default (systemd-coredump) instead of /bin/false. A crashing lnd/bitcoind (e.g. attacker-triggered via a daemon crash bug) then leaves a core dump containing in-memory secrets (lnd keys, macaroons, wallet passwords) persisted in /var/lib/systemd/coredump rather than discarded. Dumps remain readable only by root and the crashing user, so the practical exposure is limited to forensic persistence plus unbounded dump disk usage; the neighboring fs.suid_dumpable=0 does apply. This is a stated security control that silently does nothing (and 'quiet loglevel=0' kernel params hide the sysctl error at boot).
impact: secrets (persistence of in-memory key material to disk after a crash) / minor dos (disk fill); stated-control failure
false_positive_risk: None on the typo itself (the correct sysctl name is kernel.core_pattern). Impact is deliberately rated low: dumps are not world-readable, so no privilege boundary is crossed; the finding is the silent failure of a documented hardening control.

title: Residual TOCTOU between symlink check and install in onion-addresses copyOnionFile
evidence:
if [[ -L $src ]]; then
  echo "Error: refusing to read onion hostname via symlink: $src" >&2
  exit 1
fi
install -T -m 400 "$src" "$dst"
attack_scenario: A compromised tor daemon (it owns /var/lib/tor/onion/<service>) could flip the hostname file between a regular file and a symlink in the microsecond gap between the -L test and install's open(), causing the root script (CAP_DAC_OVERRIDE) to copy an arbitrary root-readable file into a mode-400 file later chowned to the operator/service user. Not reported as a vulnerability: the attacker must win a blind race with exactly one attempt per onion-addresses run (tor restart), and the payoff file is only readable by the *target* user, so exfiltration additionally requires compromising that user - the chain does not reach an attacker goal on its own. The M-4 fix is otherwise solid (fail-closed symlink refusal, root-only population before chown, chown -h).
impact: none demonstrated without an additional compromise; noted as a residual gap in an explicitly symlink-hardened script
false_positive_risk: The race may be practically unwinnable (blind, one shot per service run, no feedback channel for the attacker), which is why this is info rather than low.
recommendation: If parity with the threat model is desired, read the hostname via a single open with O_NOFOLLOW (e.g. a small python/perl one-liner or 'install' replaced by an openat2-based copy) so the check and the read are one syscall.

title: lnd macaroon root ExecStartPost still symlink-raceable: mktemp is in the lnd-owned $RUNTIME_DIRECTORY (no sticky bit)
evidence:
RuntimeDirectoryMode = "711";  /* /run/lnd: lnd:lnd, rwx--x--x, NO sticky bit */
...
macaroonTmp=$(${pkgs.coreutils}/bin/mktemp "$RUNTIME_DIRECTORY/.${macaroon}.XXXXXX")
${curl} ... | ${pkgs.jq}/bin/jq -c '.macaroon' | ${pkgs.xxd}/bin/xxd -p -r > "$macaroonTmp"
${pkgs.coreutils}/bin/chmod ug=r,o= "$macaroonTmp"
chown ${cfg.macaroons.${macaroon}.user}: "$macaroonTmp"
${pkgs.coreutils}/bin/mv -f "$macaroonTmp" "$macaroonPath"
attack_scenario: Attacker has compromised the lnd service (RCE as the `lnd` user) - the canonical threat for an LN node holding funds (lnd has had RCE CVEs). Goal: escalate to root to read the lnd wallet seed, bitcoind wallet, and all macaroons, then steal funds. On every lnd (re)start, systemd runs ExecStartPost = `+`-prefixed rootScript (runs as ROOT). For each custom macaroon (e.g. btcpayserver's, enabled by lnd+btcpayserver) it does: mktemp /run/lnd/.btcpayserver.XXXXXX; curl lnd's own REST /v1/macaroon | jq | xxd -p -r > $macaroonTmp; chmod ug=r,o= $macaroonTmp; chown btcpayserver: $macaroonTmp; mv -f $macaroonTmp /run/lnd/btcpayserver.macaroon. /run/lnd is the service RuntimeDirectory: mode 0711, owned by lnd, NO sticky bit, so the compromised lnd can unlink ANY entry (including root-owned ones) and create symlinks there. RELIABLE primitive: lnd makes its own REST response to the curl slow (seconds). During that wait it unlinks $macaroonTmp and replaces it with a symlink to e.g. /etc/nix-bitcoin-secrets/bitcoin-rpcpassword-privileged or /etc/shadow. The root script's subsequent `chmod ug=r,o= $macaroonTmp` and `chown btcpayserver: $macaroonTmp` both follow the symlink and act as root on the target: the privileged bitcoind RPC password (or /etc/shadow) becomes btcpayserver:btcpayserver mode 0440. A compromised internet-facing btcpayserver can now read it -> privileged bitcoind RPC (wallet sendtoaddress -> funds) or crack root's shadow hash -> root. LIKELY-WINNABLE primitive (direct root RCE, no second compromise needed): lnd instead swaps $macaroonTmp for a symlink to /root/.ssh/authorized_keys or /etc/cron.d/pwn BEFORE the shell opens the `> $macaroonTmp` redirection. Because inotify IN_CREATE fires at mktemp's O_CREAT - before mktemp even returns the name to the shell - an lnd watcher has a head start over the shell's (pipe + 3x fork + xxd-child open) sequence; lnd also controls the curl response body, so the bytes written through the symlink to the target are attacker-controlled. Root writes attacker bytes to /root/.ssh/authorized_keys -> attacker SSHes in as root -> exfiltrates lnd seed + bitcoind wallet -> steals all funds. lnd can retry the race by killing itself (Restart=on-failure re-runs ExecStartPost).
impact: Privilege escalation from compromised lnd service user to root (goal 2), enabling theft of lnd wallet seed + bitcoind wallet (goal 1) and exfiltration of all macaroons/TLS keys/RPC creds (goal 3); reliable sub-primitive also enables cross-service secret theft via btcpayserver and DoS of any service by chowning its critical files away.
false_positive_risk: The reliable chown/chmod-as-root primitive depends only on lnd owning /run/lnd with no sticky bit (confirmed: RuntimeDirectoryMode="711", systemd chowns RuntimeDirectory to the service User) and on lnd controlling curl's response time (it is lnd's own REST server) - both solid. The critical direct-root-RCE path depends on winning the mktemp->redirection-open race; I could not empirically reproduce it in this sandbox because inotifywait is not installed, so the 'likely winnable' claim rests on the IN_CREATE-head-start argument rather than a demonstrated exploit. If the write race proves unwinnable in practice, the finding still holds at high severity via the reliable chown/chmod primitive (boundary break + cross-service chain + DoS).
recommendation: mktemp the macaroon in a directory the untrusted lnd user cannot write to - a root-owned, mode-0700 directory (e.g. a separate root-owned runtime dir under /run created in ExecStartPre, NOT /run/lnd) - so lnd can neither predict the name nor unlink the temp file. chmod/chown the temp there, then atomically `mv` (rename) into /run/lnd; rename does not follow the destination symlink, so the final placement stays safe. Do not use $RUNTIME_DIRECTORY for root-script temp files. The current `umask ug=r,o=` and explicit `chmod ug=r,o=` are fine; the defect is solely the temp-file directory ownership.
